title: Idempotency and Delivery Guarantees
summary: A retry should not mean a second charge. Make repeated delivery safe by defining the business effect, its transaction boundary and how long you remember it.
body:
Imagine a worker charges a customer and crashes before acknowledging its message. The broker redelivers the message. Should the customer be charged again? A delivery guarantee alone cannot answer that business question. Interviewers raise this in payments, ordering, ticketing, notification and any queue-based design: whenever you add a retry or a queue, expect "what if this runs twice?".

## Separate delivery from effect

At-most-once processing can avoid retries and lose work. At-least-once delivery retries unacknowledged work and can repeat it. Some systems provide exactly-once guarantees within a particular transaction or processing boundary, but that does not automatically extend to an external payment or email API.

An operation is idempotent when repeating the same logical request does not apply its intended effect again. This is not the same as making every request for the same amount a duplicate: two legitimate purchases may have identical bodies and still be distinct operations. Some operations are naturally idempotent (`SET status = 'shipped'`, `PUT` of a full resource, delete by ID); others (`balance = balance - 10`, "send email", "append row") need a key or a recorded state transition to become safe.

| Delivery mode | When progress is recorded | Failure outcome | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| At-most-once | Before doing the work | Crash loses the work | Metrics samples, best-effort notifications |
| At-least-once | After doing the work | Crash repeats the work | Default for queues and streams |
| Effectively-once | Work and progress recorded atomically, or effect deduplicated | Repeat is detected and skipped | Payments, inventory, ledgers |

## Scope and bind a request key

A client generates a key for one logical operation and reuses it on retries. Bind the key to the authenticated tenant, operation and a canonical request fingerprint. A key reused with different parameters should produce an explicit conflict, not return an unrelated success.

Enforce uniqueness atomically, for example with a database unique constraint on `(tenant_id, operation, key)`. A separate 'check then insert' sequence races under concurrency. Define pending, completed and failed states so a second caller knows whether to wait, retry or receive the recorded response.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as API
    participant DB as Database
    C->>API: POST /orders, Idempotency-Key k1
    API->>DB: INSERT key k1 as pending, hash of body
    DB-->>API: inserted
    API->>DB: create order and store response for k1, one transaction
    API--xC: response lost on network
    C->>API: retry POST /orders, Idempotency-Key k1
    API->>DB: INSERT key k1
    DB-->>API: unique violation, k1 completed
    API-->>C: same stored response, no new order
```

The first attempt claims key `k1` with a unique insert, then creates the order and records the response in the same transaction. The response never reaches the client, so it retries with the same key. The insert now fails on the unique constraint, the API sees that `k1` is completed with a matching body hash, and returns the stored response instead of creating a second order. If the retry arrived while `k1` was still pending, the API would return a "request in progress" status (for example 409) and the client would back off. If the body hash differed, the API would reject the reuse of the key.

## Put the effect inside the right boundary

If the business write and the deduplication record live in the same database, commit them in one transaction. If a worker records 'done' before changing the balance, a crash can lose the effect; if it changes the balance and records 'done' later, a crash can repeat the effect.

An external provider cannot normally join that local transaction. Use its idempotency contract where available, keep a durable record of the intended operation and reconcile uncertain outcomes. A transactional outbox can atomically record a local state change and an event to publish, but the dispatcher may publish twice. Consumers must still handle duplicates.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    API["Order service"] -->|"one transaction"| DB[("orders + outbox tables")]
    DB --> RELAY["Outbox relay or CDC"]
    RELAY -->|"may publish twice"| K[["Event stream"]]
    K --> CON["Consumer"]
    CON -->|"insert event_id unique, apply effect, same txn"| CDB[("Consumer DB")]
```

The order service writes the order row and an outbox row describing the event in one local transaction, so neither can exist without the other. A relay polls the outbox (or a CDC connector reads the database log) and publishes to the stream, marking rows as sent. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it publishes again, so the stream is at-least-once. The consumer makes that harmless by recording the event ID in a processed-events table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as its own effect: a duplicate event hits the constraint and is skipped. This replaces the fragile dual write of "commit to the database, then publish to Kafka" from application code.

## Expiry is part of correctness

A deduplication key is useful only while the system remembers it. Retention must cover the supported retry and redelivery window. A reused key after expiry may be a new operation. Document that boundary rather than promising duplicate protection forever. As a sizing example, 2,000 payments per second with 24-hour key retention is about 173 million keys; at roughly 200 bytes each including the stored response that is around 35 GB, which argues for a TTL index or a partitioned table that drops whole days.

## Common interview mistakes

- Claiming the broker or Kafka provides exactly-once delivery to an external system.
- Generating the idempotency key on the server per attempt, so every retry looks new.
- Deduplicating on request body alone and blocking legitimate repeat purchases.
- Checking for the key and inserting it in two separate steps.
- Treating a timeout from a payment provider as a failure and charging again without querying the provider or reusing its idempotency key.

## How to use it in an interview

Name the duplicate source (client retry, broker redelivery, relay republish), then the boundary where you stop it: "Clients send an `Idempotency-Key`; we enforce it with a unique index in the orders database in the same transaction as the order. Downstream consumers dedupe on event ID. Calls to the payment provider reuse our payment ID as their idempotency key, and a reconciliation job resolves payments stuck in 'unknown'." State the retention window. Expect follow-ups: "what if the client retries while the first request is still running?", "what if the key is reused with a different amount?", and "how long do you keep keys?".

## Interview exercise

Draw a queue consumer that updates a wallet in one database. Mark the transaction and the acknowledgement. Then replace the wallet update with an external payment call. Identify the new uncertain state and describe how the same operation can be safely retried or reconciled.

## Further reading

- [Stripe's idempotent request documentation](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) is a concrete provider contract. Its parameter checking and retention rules illustrate why 'use a UUID' is only the start of the design, not the whole solution.
- [Apache Kafka documentation: message delivery semantics](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#semantics) explains where Kafka's exactly-once guarantees begin and end.
keyTakeaways: At-least-once delivery means consumers must expect duplicates.
Bind an idempotency key to caller, operation and payload, and enforce it atomically.
Local transactions do not automatically cover external side effects.
State the retention and retry window of any deduplication guarantee.
